questions.topic: What a labour shortage changed besides headcount
questions.learningObjective: Identify what a labour shortage changed besides the size of the workforce.
questions.stem: The planner's memo notes that three of the city's four foundries lost a third of their skilled moulders to the army in eighteen months while orders rose by half.

options.text: The organisation of work, since skilled jobs were broken into simpler operations
The hours of work, which fell across the trades as employers spread the work about
options.misconception: Reads a shortage as an employer decision to shorten hours

options.text: The price of output, which rose because the shortage made every article dearer to make
options.misconception: Assumes a labour shortage must raise the price of output

options.text: The location of the works, which moved to the coast to shorten the haul to the docks
options.misconception: Finds a relocation the memo nowhere records

questions.explanation: The memo pairs a loss of skilled men with a rising order book, which forces employers to reorganise the work rather than merely replace the men. The other readings need a fall in hours.
questions.hint: Look at what the firms had to change, not what they lost.

questions.subject: US_HISTORY
questions.topic: What a labour shortage changed besides headcount
questions.learningObjective: Explain what a comparison of output per worker shows about a labour shortage.
questions.stem: A paragraph of the memo compares the city's output per worker in 1915 and 1918 and notes that the wages of the surviving workers rose by a third.

answer.exemplar: Output per worker rising while headcount fell shows that the city reorganised rather than simply shrank, dividing skilled jobs and putting more work through each remaining pair of hands. The comparison cannot show where the gains came from. Machinery bought, longer hours, faster working and the dilution of skill all produce the same figure, and the memo records the result without separating the causes.

questions.explanation: A rising output per worker alongside fewer men indicates the work was reorganised rather than simply abandoned. The figures cannot separate machinery from longer hours or diluted skill.
questions.hint: A single ratio can hide several different causes.

questions.topic: What a labour shortage changed besides headcount
questions.learningObjective: Draw a conclusion about a labour shortage from an enclosed letter.

stimulus.body: The works lost eleven of its thirty-two turners in the first quarter. We did not replace them as turners. We bought a lathe that one man can work, we put women and boys on the simpler cuts, and we kept two of the old turners to set the machines. The output of the shop is the same as it was and the hours are longer, and I do not think the same shop can be run on a third of the men next year.

options.misconception: Finds a closure the enclosure does not describe

options.text: The shop was taken over by the government because private firms could not manage
options.misconception: Invents a takeover to explain a simple reorganisation

questions.explanation: The manager replaced skilled turners with machine operators, put less experienced hands on simpler cuts and worked longer hours, so the shape of the work changed. Output was unchanged.

questions.topic: What a labour shortage changed besides headcount
questions.learningObjective: Assess the claim a survey in the memo supports about a labour shortage.

stimulus.body: A survey of the city's building trades shows the same pattern in every one of them. The men left for the army, the work did not stop, and the houses went up more slowly. questions.explanation: The survey shows work continuing with fewer, differently organised hands at the same rate of pay, which is a reorganisation rather than a simple loss. No wage cut appears.

questions.subject: US_HISTORY
questions.topic: A war office report on a substitute material
questions.learningObjective: Explain what a war office expected of a substitute material.
questions.stem: The war office report enclosed with the memo records that a material for shells had to be made from a domestic substitute that behaved differently in cold weather.

answer.exemplar: The war office turned to the substitute because the imported material could no longer be counted on in the quantity formerly obtained, and the report therefore treats the change as a question of securing shells rather than of saving money. What the report exposes is the limit of that reasoning: the substitute had to be specified to a new standard, tested against the old one, and ordered in quantities the domestic trade had never produced, so the replacement of a material began a second procurement problem rather than closing the first.

questions.explanation: The report treats the substitute as a way of securing shells when the imported material could not be relied on. It also shows new work in specifying, testing and ordering at scale.
questions.hint: The report is about shells first and prices second.

questions.topic: A war office report on a substitute material

stimulus.body: The material formerly obtained from abroad cannot be counted on in the quantity formerly obtained, and the war office has directed that production shall be placed with firms able to work to the new specification. questions.topic: A war office report on a substitute material
questions.learningObjective: Assess what a works note shows about the limits of substitution.

stimulus.body: We have been told to use the cheaper stuff, and we will, but the plant was set up for the other material. The presses run too hot on it and the pieces come out uneven, so we are throwing away about one in seven and running the presses slower to make up for it. The accountant would rather we did not throw anything away, and the works manager would rather we did not slow the presses down.

options.text: Substitution works on price, but the plant built for the old material limits the gain
Substitution works on price, and the plant built for the old material improved the gain
options.misconception: Ignores the waste and the slower presses the note records

options.text: Substitution failed because the cheaper material could not be bought in the quantity needed

options.text: Substitution failed because the war office refused to let the trade use the old material
options.misconception: Misreads the direction to substitute as a refusal

questions.explanation: The cheaper material was obtainable, but the presses were wrong for it, so a seventh of the output was scrapped and the presses ran slow. Substitution bought price at the cost of waste.

questions.topic: A signals report on a read enemy cipher
questions.learningObjective: Draw a conclusion about reading a cipher from a signals report.

stimulus.body: The station at the island has been reading its own traffic for six months and has produced a useful body of material, but it cannot see that the same keys are used on two circuits that the station never hears together. A single station's view is a single station's view. We recommend that the intercepts from all stations be sent to one place, worked as a single body, and the results returned to the stations in a standard form so that the men on the ground are not left to work the same traffic twice.

questions.stem: The signals report is filed in the planner's memo. What does it show about reading an enemy cipher?

options.text: The value of the reading depended on combining traffic that separate stations could not see together
The value of the reading depended on the station with the best trained officer working alone
options.misconception: Credits one officer's skill, not the argument for combining

options.text: The value of the reading depended on gathering more traffic than any one station could hold
options.misconception: Confuses the problem of volume with that of separation

options.text: The value of the reading depended on returning material to the stations unchanged and quickly
options.misconception: Treats speed of return as the report's chief recommendation

questions.explanation: The island station had useful material but could not see keys shared across circuits it never heard, so the report argues for one body of traffic. The others credit skill, volume or speed.
questions.hint: The report says what a single station's view could not show.

questions.subject: US_HISTORY
questions.topic: A signals report on a read enemy cipher
questions.learningObjective: Determine what a signals instruction requires of stations.

stimulus.body: All station officers will note that the reading of a foreign code is not a matter for private experiment. A key learned at one station has no value at another until the traffic is worked as one body, and two stations working the same book independently will twice miss the repetition that gives the key away. Any material considered to have a bearing on the enemy's movements will be sent by the prescribed channel on the day it is obtained, with the hour noted at the foot of the form.

options.text: That readings be reported through one channel in a common form, rather than kept locally
That each station report privately to the officer who found the material, and no further

options.text: That stations withhold anything they believe to be of value until it can be confirmed
options.misconception: Inverts the instruction to report on the day it is obtained

options.text: That stations exchange their working directly with one another and skip the central office
options.misconception: Ignores the central office the instruction builds

questions.explanation: The instruction forbids private experiment, says a key has no value until the traffic is worked as one body, and requires reporting by the prescribed channel. The others invert it.
questions.hint: Note the words about the prescribed channel and the day.

questions.subject: US_HISTORY
questions.topic: A signals report on a read enemy cipher
questions.learningObjective: Explain why a combined record of traffic was worth more than either part.
questions.stem: One member's note compares two stations that had read the same enemy code for months and set out their separate holdings of the traffic.

answer.exemplar: Each station held a fragment of the enemy's correspondence and neither could tell whether its fragment was typical, because the repetitions that show a habit lay in traffic the other station held. Combined, the two records showed which phrases recurred, which never appeared, and which changed with the enemy's preparations, and a pattern of that kind could be acted on while a single fragment could not. That is why the report insists that the traffic be worked as a single body of material.

questions.explanation: Neither station could judge whether its fragment was typical, because the habit lay in traffic the other held, and only the combined record showed what recurred. A pattern could be acted on.
questions.hint: Ask what each station could not see about its own material.

questions.topic: Range and endurance in a Pacific battle
questions.learningObjective: Draw a conclusion about range and endurance from a naval note.

stimulus.kind: extract from the planner's naval notes
stimulus.body: The enemy's aircraft reached far enough to be a nuisance well beyond the reach of our own, which is the whole difficulty in a fight of this kind. A fleet that keeps itself beyond the enemy's reach cannot fight, and a fleet that comes inside it must accept that the enemy will find it first unless something keeps their eyes turned the other way. Our two carriers went in from the north-west with the wind, which is the only reason the enemy did not see them first.

questions.explanation: The extract states the dilemma: staying beyond reach means not fighting, and coming inside it means risking discovery first, which the wind and the approach reduced.

The arguments show a settlement whose machinery was detailed and conventional, with the weight placed in a single article whose interpretation was left open. That openness was the source of the dispute, because the article could be read narrowly or broadly and both readings had serious supporters.

questions.topic: A war office report on a substitute material
questions.learningObjective: Explain what a comparison of costs at three volumes shows about substitution.
questions.stem: A war office report enclosed with the memo compares the cost of the imported material with the cost of the domestic substitute at three different volumes of production.

answer.exemplar: At the volume required for ordinary trade the substitute was dearer than the imported article, and only when the war office guaranteed a large order did the price fall below it, which shows that the change in cost came from the scale of the order and not from a naturally cheaper material. The comparison does not show the cost of the plant changes the new material demanded, nor the waste the works manager described, so it measures the purchase and not the whole of the change.

questions.subject: US_HISTORY
questions.topic: Why a convoy travels at its slowest ship
questions.learningObjective: Establish what convoy instructions show about a convoy's pace.

stimulus.body: Sailers in a convoy will keep the station assigned to them and will not exceed the speed of the flagship, which is the speed of the slowest ship fitted to act as flagship. Should any vessel be unable to maintain the assigned speed, the master is to report the fact at once so that the commodore may decide whether to reduce the speed of the whole, to place the vessel in another division, or to dispatch her under escort. Masters are not to attempt to leave the convoy, and are not to take it upon themselves to act upon a different station.

options.text: That the commodore must raise the speed of the whole whenever a ship falls behind
options.misconception: Reverses the decision the commodore is given

questions.explanation: The instructions tie the convoy's speed to the flagship, which is the slowest ship fitted to take that role, and reserve any change to the commodore.
questions.hint: Who decides what happens when a ship cannot keep up?

questions.subject: US_HISTORY
questions.topic: Sloping the hull and turning out numbers
questions.learningObjective: Assess what a yard manager's note shows about turning out numbers.

stimulus.body: We are not building thirty different ships. We are building one ship thirty times over, and every yard in the country is doing the same, which is why the drawings can be bought ready-made from a bureau in another city. The steel comes in bundles cut to the frame spacing, the boilers come from the same works in the same lots, and the men learn the job in a fortnight. What has changed is not the ship but the number of them, and even that is now limited by the number of slips we have and the plate we can get.

options.misconception: Treats a supply of drawings as a delay

questions.explanation: One design, ready-made drawings, bundled plate and boilers in standard lots and a fortnight of training multiplied the number of hulls, but the slips and plate remained the limit.
questions.hint: Read the manager's final sentence before the earlier ones.

questions.subject: US_HISTORY
questions.topic: What a labour shortage changed besides headcount
questions.learningObjective: Explain what the end of the shortage shows about the earlier reorganisation.
questions.stem: A later section of the memo returns to the labour shortage and describes what happened when the war ended and the men came back to the trades.

answer.exemplar: The men who came back found their jobs divided and their rates of pay changed, which shows that the reorganisation of work was not a temporary expedient but a change in the shape of the trade, and that the war had left the trades organised in a way their peace would not undo at once. The return of the men also produced a surplus of hands, which is a fact about the end of the war rather than about the shortage, and the memo's silence on the older workers' places leaves open whether the men who returned were ever given the work they had left.

questions.explanation: The assembly was kept to make the conduct of states a matter of public argument, and being named was expected to restrain a state without enforcement.
questions.hint: The trades did not go back to their old shape at the end.

questions.subject: US_HISTORY
questions.topic: Range and endurance in a Pacific battle
questions.learningObjective: Establish what a naval note shows about range and endurance.

stimulus.kind: note in the planner's naval appendix
stimulus.body: The two things that decided the afternoon were the fuel the fleet had left and the fact that the enemy was looking the other way. A fleet with more fuel and the same surprise would have had the same result; so would the same fuel and better surprise. What the enemy's reach gave us was the shape of the approach, and what the approach gave us was the two hours in which nothing was expected of us. It is worth recording that neither side's fleet was larger than the other by a single hull, and that the man who saw the position first did most of the work.
